study.title: Isaiah 25 Praise to God who judges, saves and overcomes death
study.overview: Isaiah 25 is a song of exaltation to the LORD after the vision of judgment upon the world. The chapter celebrates that God overthrows oppressive cities, protects the needy, prepares a banquet of salvation for all peoples and removes forever the death and shame of his people. At the same time, he states that the pride of the enemies will not remain: God's protection for his own is also the ruin of the strongholds of those who resist him.

outline.title: Praise to God who acts faithfully and humbles the violent
outline.explanation: The prophet begins by worshipping the LORD for his wonderful deeds and for his ancient counsels, which are fulfilled with fidelity and truth. He then recalls that God has turned strong cities into ruins and that this leads to powerful peoples glorifying it. The central contrast is between the violent, who oppress, and God, who becomes the stronghold of the poor, refuge of the needy and moderator of the arrogance of the enemies.

outline.title: The banquet of God and the victory over death
outline.explanation: On the mount of the LORD, God prepares a rich banquet for all peoples, an image of generous provision and saving communion. The text speaks of the removal of the funerary veil that covers the nations and declares that God will destroy death forever. The consequence is universal comfort, wiped tears and the humiliation of God's people finally removed.

outline.title: The joy of the redeemed and the fall of enemy pride
outline.explanation: On that day the people will proclaim that the LORD is their God and that their salvation was awaited with hope. In contrast, Moab is portrayed as utterly slaughtered under the hand of the LORD, with his proud crushed and his strongholds knocked down to the dust. The chapter ends by showing that the humility of faith and rebellious arrogance have opposite destinies before God.

study.context: The chapter is presented as a response of praise after previous announcements of judgment. The given notes place the passage in continuity with the section called the "little apocalypse" section and observe that some elements may refer to the historical deliveries of the people of God, but also point to a broader and more definitive fulfillment. The text, however, does not explicitly identify a unique historical event here; therefore, it is appropriate to read the chapter as a prophetic vision of judgment and salvation that reaches both the present and the future hope.
study.theology: Chapter theology highlights four central themes. First, God is faithful to his old counsels: what he promised through the prophets is fulfilled at the right time. Second, the LORD is a defender of the poor and the needy; his strength does not serve to magnify the arrogant, but to support the weak and overthrow violence. Third, God's salvation is abundant and universal in scope: the banquet is offered to the peoples, and the hope of God's people is an answer of faith and joy. Fourth, divine victory is deeper than any political liberation, as it includes the annihilation of death and shame. Thus, the chapter combines judgment against the proud with comfort for those who wait in the LORD; and many Christian interpreters see in this promise a horizon that points to the resurrection and consummation of redemption in Christ.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter is divided between praise to God's judgment, salvation, and final triumph of God's people; verses 1-5, 11-12 celebrate judgment, while 6-9 proclaim salvation.
The banquet and promise that death will be swallowed up points beyond temporal deliveries and find their full fulfillment in the resurrection and victory of Christ.
God's ancient counsels mean that all the previous statements made by the prophets will be fulfilled at the proper time.

questions: What changes in our worship when we remember that God not only consoles, but also overthrows structures of pride and violence?
How does the image of God's banquet correct our idea of salvation as something only individual and private?
How will the promise that God will wipe tears and destroy death strengthen perseverance amidst the present suffering?
study.practice: Practice a prayer of gratitude based on the chapter: recognize a concrete act of God's faithfulness in your life, confess any confidence in human forces and give him his anguish. Then try to act as a reflection of this God: be a refuge for someone in need, offer comfort to those weeps and witness with humility that the final hope is in the Lord. It is also worth reading this chapter in community, as a song of hope, especially in the face of grief, fear or oppression.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided allow some historical key readings and others in eschatological key, but do not fix a single historical context for all the details. Verse 11 is recognized as obscure in the notes, especially in the image of the swimmer; therefore, the explanation must be kept with caution. Moreover, references to fulfillment in Christ, the resurrection and consummation of the gospel are theological interpretations present in the commentators, not statements explicitly stated in the text of Isaiah 25.
